text: What he wanted was south of the city.
On the advice of Senator Stephen Douglas, who told him to plant every spare dollar south of downtown, he started buying.

He talked the widow of a man named Watson into selling him sixty acres, sold off other ground to pay for it, and kept assembling until by 1853 he held about 300 acres along the lake, between what we now call 51st and 55th streets.
It sat roughly six miles south of downtown, far enough that most Chicagoans had never bothered to walk it.
It was prairie and sand and shoreline, the kind of land people called worthless to your face.
Cornell put thousands of dollars into it anyway, and the first thing he gave it was not a road or a house.
It was a name borrowed from somewhere richer.
He called it Hyde Park, after the park in London, because the name carried the sound of elegant estates and old money.
He wanted the people he hoped to sell to, the comfortable Chicago businessmen and their families, to hear the name and picture themselves somewhere finer than the crowded streets they lived on.
He was selling an idea before he had sold a single lot.
The idea was room to breathe, a clean place near the water, a few miles from the smoke and the noise and the rising rents of the packed city.
In a town where everyone lived practically on top of one another, that promise was worth real money, and Cornell knew it.
